**Article 248:** A guardian or curator shall be appointed for the child whenever paternity and maternity have been judicially determined against the opposition of both father and mother. The same shall apply to the child whose parents do not have the right to exercise parental authority or whose filiation is not legally determined with respect to either the father or the mother.

**Article 249:** The legal determination of paternity or maternity puts an end to the guardianship in which the minor child may be and gives the father or mother, as appropriate, parental authority over their property.

payloads.title: § 2\. Of the Legal Right of Enjoyment over the Children's Property and Its Administration
payloads.content:
**Article 250:** Parental authority confers the legal right of enjoyment over all the child's property, except for the following:

1. Property acquired by the child in the exercise of any employment, office, profession, or industry. The property covered by this number forms their professional or industrial special property.
2. Property acquired by the child by way of gift, inheritance, or legacy, when the donor or testator has stipulated that the person exercising parental authority shall not have the enjoyment or administration; has imposed the condition of obtaining emancipation, or has expressly provided that the child shall have the enjoyment of this property, and
3. Inheritances or legacies that have passed to the child due to incapacity, indignity, or disinheritance of the father or mother who has parental authority.

In these cases, the enjoyment shall correspond to the child or the other parent, in accordance with articles 251 and 253\.

The enjoyment over the child's mines shall be limited to half of the products and the parent exercising parental authority shall be liable to the child for the other half.

**Article 251:** The child shall be regarded as of legal age for the administration and enjoyment of their professional or industrial special property, without prejudice to the provisions of article 254\.

**Article 252:** The legal right of enjoyment is a personal right consisting of the faculty to use the child's property and receive its fruits, with the obligation to preserve the form and substance of said property and to restore them, if they are not fungible; or with the obligation to return an equal quantity and quality of the same kind, or to pay their value, if they are fungible.

The father or mother is not obliged, by reason of their legal right of enjoyment, to provide security for preservation or restitution, nor to make a solemn inventory, without prejudice to the provisions of article 124\. But if they do not make a solemn inventory, they shall keep a detailed description of the property from when they begin to enjoy it.

When this right corresponds to the married mother in a conjugal partnership, this shall be considered partially separated as to property with respect to its exercise and what is obtained from it. This separation shall be governed by the rules of article 150\.

If parental authority is exercised jointly by both parents and no other distribution has been agreed, the legal right of enjoyment shall be divided between them in equal parts.

The legal right of enjoyment is also called the legal usufruct of the father or mother over the child's property. To the extent appropriate to its nature, it shall be supplementarily governed by the rules of Title IX of Book II.

**Article 253:** One who exercises the legal right of enjoyment over the child's property shall have their administration, and one who is deprived of the latter shall also be deprived of the former.

If the father or mother who has parental authority cannot exercise the legal right of enjoyment over one or more of the child's property, this shall pass to the other; and if both are impeded, full ownership shall belong to the child and a curator shall be appointed for their administration.

**Article 254:** In no case may the child's real property, even if belonging to their professional or industrial special property, nor their hereditary rights, be alienated or encumbered without judicial authorization with knowledge of the case.

**Article 255:** No donation of any part of the child's property may be made, nor may it be leased for a long time, nor may an inheritance devolved to the child be accepted or repudiated, except in the manner and with the limitations imposed on guardians and curators.

**Article 256:** The father or mother is responsible, in the administration of the child's property, even for slight fault.

The responsibility towards the child extends to the property and the fruits, in those child's property in which they have administration but not enjoyment, and is limited to the property when they exercise both faculties over the property.

**Article 257:** There shall be a right to remove the administration of the child's property from the father or mother, or both, when they have been guilty of fraud, or of habitual gross negligence, and so established by judicial sentence, which shall be sub-registered in the margin of the child's birth registration.

They shall also lose the administration whenever parental authority is suspended, in accordance with article 267\.

**Article 258:** If one of the parents is deprived of the administration of the property, the other shall have it; if neither of them has it, full ownership shall belong to the child, and a curator shall be appointed for their administration.

**Article 259:** At the end of parental authority, parents shall inform their children of the administration they have exercised over their property.

payloads.title: § 3\. Of the Legal Representation of Children
payloads.content:
**Article 260:** The acts and contracts of the child not authorized by the father or mother who has them under parental authority, or by the joint curator, as applicable, shall bind the child only in their professional or industrial special property.

But they may not take money on interest, nor buy on credit (except in the ordinary course of said special property) without written authorization from the mentioned persons. And if they do so, they shall not be bound by these contracts, except to the extent of the benefit they derived from them.

**Article 261:** If there is a conjugal partnership between the parents, the acts and contracts the child enters into outside their professional or industrial special property and which the father or mother exercising parental authority authorizes or ratifies in writing, or those they perform in representation of the child, directly bind the father or mother in accordance with the provisions of that property regime and, subsidiarily, the child, to the extent of the benefit the child derived from said acts or contracts.

If there is no conjugal partnership, these acts and contracts only bind, in the manner indicated in the preceding paragraph, the father or mother who has intervened. The foregoing does not prevent the father or mother from seeking reimbursement from the other parent, to the extent they were legally required to provide for the child's needs.

**Article 262:** The adult minor does not need authorization from their parents to dispose of their property by testamentary act to take effect after their death, nor to recognize children.

**Article 263:** Whenever the child has to litigate as plaintiff against the father or mother who exercises parental authority, it shall be necessary to obtain the court's leave and the judge, upon granting it, shall appoint a curator for the lawsuit.

The father or mother who, having parental authority, litigates with the child, whether as plaintiff or defendant, shall provide them with expenses for the lawsuit, which the court shall regulate incidentally, considering the amount and importance of what is at issue and the economic capacity of the parties.

**Article 264:** The child may not appear in court, as plaintiff, against a third party, unless authorized or represented by the father or mother who exercises parental authority, or by both, if they exercise it jointly.

If the father, mother, or both refuse their consent to the child for the civil action they wish to bring against a third party, or if they are unable to give it, the judge may supply it, and in doing so shall appoint a curator for the lawsuit for the child.

**Article 265:** In civil actions against the child, the plaintiff must address the father or mother who has parental authority, to authorize or represent the child in the lawsuit. If both exercise parental authority jointly, it shall suffice to address one of them.

If the father or mother cannot or will not give their authorization or representation, the judge may supply it, and shall appoint a curator for the lawsuit for the child.

**Article 266:** Parental intervention shall not be necessary to proceed criminally against the child; but the father or mother who has parental authority shall be obliged to provide them with the necessary assistance for their defense.

payloads.title: § 4\. Of the Suspension of Parental Authority
payloads.content:
**Article 267:** Parental authority is suspended by the dementia of the father or mother who exercises it, by their minority, by being under interdiction to administer their property, and by their prolonged absence or other physical impediment, from which serious harm to the child's interests results, which the absent or impeded parent does not remedy.

In these cases, parental authority shall be exercised by the other parent, with respect to whom it shall be suspended for the same reasons. If suspended with respect to both, the child shall be subject to guardianship.

**Article 268:** The suspension of parental authority shall be decreed by the judge with knowledge of the case, and after hearing the child's relatives and the defender of minors; except when it concerns the minority of the father or mother, in which case suspension shall occur by operation of law.

The judge, in the child's interest, may decree that the father or mother regain parental authority when the cause that motivated the suspension has ceased.

The resolution that decrees or sets aside the suspension shall be sub-registered in the margin of the child's birth registration.

payloads.title: § 5\. Of Emancipation
payloads.content:
**Article 269:** Emancipation is an event that puts an end to the parental authority of the father, mother, or both, as the case may be. It may be legal or judicial.

**Article 270:** Legal emancipation occurs:

1. By the death of the father or mother, unless the other parent is to exercise parental authority;
2. By the decree granting provisional possession, or definitive possession as applicable, of the property of the disappeared father or mother, unless the other parent is to exercise parental authority;
3. Eliminated.
4. By the child reaching the age of eighteen.

**Article 271:** Judicial emancipation is effected by judge's decree:

1. When the father or mother habitually mistreats the child, unless the other parent is to exercise parental authority;
2. When the father or mother has abandoned the child, except in the exception case of the preceding number;
3. When by final judgment the father or mother has been convicted of a crime deserving afflictive punishment, even if a pardon is granted for the sentence, unless, considering the nature of the crime, the judge considers there is no risk to the child's interest, or the other parent assumes parental authority, and
4. In case of physical or moral inability of the father or mother, if the other parent is not to exercise parental authority.

The judicial resolution decreeing emancipation shall be sub-registered in the margin of the child's birth registration.

**Article 272:** Every emancipation, once effected, is irrevocable.

Excepted from this rule is emancipation by presumed death or by judicial sentence based on the parent's moral inability, which may be set aside by the judge, at the request of the respective parent, when their existence is reliably proven or that the inability has ceased, as applicable, and moreover it is shown that recovery of parental authority is in the child's interests. The judicial resolution that grants revocation shall only produce effects from its sub-registration in the margin of the child's birth registration. Revocation of emancipation may proceed only once.

**Article 273:** The emancipated minor child shall be subject to guardianship.

**Articles 274-296:** Repealed.

payloads.title: § 1\. Definitions and General Rules
payloads.content:
**Article 338:** Guardianships and curatorships are charges imposed on certain persons in favor of those who cannot direct themselves or competently administer their affairs, and who are not under the authority of a father or mother who can provide them with due protection.

The persons who exercise these charges are called guardians or curators and generally caregivers.

**Article 339:** The provisions of this title and the following two are subject to the modifications and exceptions that will be expressed in the special titles of guardianship and each kind of curatorship.

**Article 340:** Guardianship and general curatorships extend not only to the property but to the person of the individuals subject to them.

**Article 341:** Pubescents are subject to guardianship.

**Article 342:** The following are subject to general curatorship: adult minors; those who, for prodigality or dementia, have been placed under interdiction to administer their property; and the deaf or deaf-mutes who cannot make themselves clearly understood.

**Article 343:** Those appointed for the property of the absentee, the vacant estate, and the eventual rights of the unborn are called curators of property.

**Article 344:** Those appointed in certain cases to persons who are under the authority of father or mother, or under guardianship or general curatorship, to exercise a separate administration, are called joint curators.

**Article 345:** A special curator is one appointed for a particular matter.

**Article 346:** Individuals subject to guardianship or curatorship are called wards.

**Article 347:** Two or more individuals may be placed under the same guardianship or curatorship, provided there is indivision of patrimonies. Once the patrimonies are divided, there shall be considered as many guardianships or curatorships as there are distinct patrimonies, even if exercised by the same person.

The same guardianship or curatorship may be exercised jointly by two or more guardians or curators.

**Article 348:** No guardian or general curator may be appointed for one who is under parental authority, except when it is suspended in one of the cases enumerated in article 267\.

A joint curator shall be appointed for the child when the father or mother are deprived of the administration of the child's property or part of it, according to article 251\.

**Article 349:** A curator shall be appointed for spouses in the same cases in which, if single, they would need a curator for the administration of their property.

**Article 350:** Generally, no guardian or curator may be appointed for one who already has one: only a joint curator may be appointed, in the cases designated by law.

**Article 351:** If the guardian or curator, alleging the excessive complexity of the ward's affairs and their insufficiency to fully administer them, requests that a curator be added, the judge may grant it, having heard the ward's relatives and the respective defender.

The judge shall then divide the administration in the manner deemed most convenient.

**Article 352:** If a gift, inheritance, or legacy is made to one who is under guardianship or curatorship, with the precise condition that the property included in the gift, inheritance, or legacy be administered by a person designated by the donor or testator, the wishes of the latter shall be followed; unless, after hearing the relatives and the respective defender, it appears more convenient for the ward to repudiate the gift, inheritance, or legacy than to accept it on those terms.

If the gift, inheritance, or legacy is accepted, and the donor or testator has not designated the person, or the designated person is not competent, the magistrate shall make the designation.

**Article 353:** Guardianships or curatorships may be testamentary, legitimate, or dativa.

Testamentary are those constituted by testamentary act.

Legitimate are those conferred by law on the relatives or spouse of the ward.

Dativa are those conferred by the magistrate.

The rules of testamentary guardianship are followed by that conferred by act between living persons, according to article 360\.

payloads.title: § 2\. Of Testamentary Guardianship or Curatorship
payloads.content:
**Article 354:** The father or mother may appoint a guardian, by will, not only for born children, but for the one still in the mother's womb, in case they are born alive.

**Article 355:** They may also appoint a curator, by will, for adult minors; and for adults of any age who are in a state of dementia, or are deaf or deaf-mutes who do not understand or make themselves clearly understood.

**Article 356:** They may also appoint a curator, by will, for the defense of the eventual rights of the unborn child.

**Article 357:** The father or mother who has been deprived of parental authority by judge's decree, according to article 271, or who by bad administration has been judicially removed from the child's guardianship, shall lack the rights conferred by the preceding articles.

The father or mother shall also lack these rights when filiation has been judicially determined against their opposition.

**Article 358:** If both the father and mother have appointed a guardian by will, the appointment made by the parent who exercised the child's parental authority shall be considered first.

**Article 359:** If it is not possible to apply the rule of the preceding article, the rules of articles 361 and 363 shall apply to the guardians appointed by the will of the father and mother.

**Article 360:** Notwithstanding the provisions of article 357, the father, mother, and any other person, may appoint a curator, by will or by act between living persons, when they give or leave to the ward any part of their property, which is not owed to them by way of legitimate share.

This curatorship shall be limited to the property given or left to the ward.

**Article 361:** Two or more guardians or curators may be appointed by will to exercise the guardianship simultaneously; and the testator shall have the faculty to divide the administration among them.

**Article 362:** If there are several wards, and the testator divides them among the appointed guardians or curators, all of them shall exercise the guardianship or curatorship jointly, as long as the patrimony remains undivided; and once the patrimony is divided, the guardianship shall be divided among them by the same fact, and they shall be independent from each other.

But the care of the person of each ward shall belong exclusively to their respective guardian or curator, even during the indivision of the patrimony.

**Article 363:** If the testator appoints several guardians or curators to exercise guardianship or curatorship jointly, and does not divide the functions among them, the judge, after hearing the ward's relatives, may entrust them to one of the appointed persons or to the number they deem sufficient, and in this second case, divide it as best suits the security of the ward's interests.

**Article 364:** Several guardians or curators may also be appointed by will to substitute or succeed one another; and once the substitution or succession is established for a particular case, it shall apply to the others in which the guardian or curator fails; unless it manifestly appears that the testator intended to limit the substitution or succession to the designated case or cases.

**Article 365:** Testamentary guardianships and curatorships admit suspensive and resolutory conditions, and designation of a certain day on which they begin or expire.

**Article 363:** If the testator appoints several guardians or curators to exercise guardianship or curatorship jointly, and does not divide the functions among them, the judge, after hearing the ward's relatives, may entrust them to one of the appointed persons or to the number they deem sufficient, and in this second case, divide it as best suits the security of the ward's interests.

**Article 364:** Several guardians or curators may also be appointed by will to substitute or succeed one another; and once the substitution or succession is established for a particular case, it shall apply to the others in which the guardian or curator fails; unless it manifestly appears that the testator intended to limit the substitution or succession to the designated case or cases.

**Article 365:** Testamentary guardianships and curatorships admit suspensive and resolutory conditions, and designation of a certain day on which they begin or expire.

payloads.title: § 3\. Of Legitimate Guardianship or Curatorship
payloads.content:
**Article 366:** Legitimate guardianship takes place when testamentary guardianship is lacking or expires.

It takes place especially when the minor is emancipated, and when parental authority is suspended by judge's decree.

**Article 367:** Those called to legitimate guardianship or curatorship are, in general:

First, the father of the ward; Second, the mother; Third, other ascendants of both sexes; Fourth, the siblings of both sexes of the ward, and the siblings of both sexes of the ward's ascendants.

If there is no place for the guardianship or curatorship of the father or mother, the judge, after hearing the ward's relatives, shall choose among the other ascendants, and in the absence of ascendants, among the collaterals here designated, the person deemed most suitable, and who presents the best guarantees; and they may also, if deemed convenient, choose more than one and divide the functions among them.

**Article 368:** The father or mother who first recognized the child not conceived nor born during marriage is called to the legitimate guardianship of the child, and if both recognized at the same time, the father.

This call shall put an end to the guardianship in which the recognized child was, except in case of inability or legitimate excuse of the one who, according to the preceding paragraph, is called to exercise it.

If filiation has not been determined or if filiation has been established judicially against the opposition of the father or mother, the child's guardianship shall be dativa.

**Article 369:** If during the pupil's status the legitimate caregiver ceases in their charge, they shall be replaced by another of the same kind.

payloads.title: § 4\. Of Dativa Guardianship or Curatorship
payloads.content:
**Article 370:** In the absence of another guardianship or curatorship, dativa guardianship applies.

**Article 371:** When for any cause the discernment of a guardianship or curatorship is delayed, or during it an impediment arises that for some time prevents the guardian or curator from continuing to exercise it, an interim guardian or curator shall be appointed by the magistrate, for as long as the delay or impediment lasts.

But if there is another guardian or curator who can supply the lack, or if it concerns appointing a guardian or curator to succeed the one currently performing the guardianship or curatorship, and they can continue in it for some time, the appointment of the interim shall not take place.

**Article 372:** The magistrate, for the election of the dativa guardian or curator, shall hear the ward's relatives, and may, if necessary, appoint two or more, and divide the functions among them, as in the case of article 363\.

If there is a joint curator, the judge may prefer them for the dativa guardianship or curatorship.

payloads.title: § 1\. Of Incapacities
payloads.content:
**I. Rules relating to physical and moral defects**

**Article 497:** The following are incapable of any guardianship or curatorship:

1. The blind;
2. The mute;
3. The demented, even if not under interdiction;
4. Bankrupts as long as they have not satisfied their creditors;
5. Those who are deprived of administering their own property for prodigality;
6. Those who lack domicile in the Republic;
7. Those who cannot read or write;
8. Those of notoriously bad conduct;
9. Those convicted of a crime deserving afflictive punishment, even if pardoned thereof;
10. Suppressed;
11. One who has been deprived of exercising parental authority according to article 271;
12. Those who by faulty or careless administration have been removed from a previous guardianship, or in the subsequent lawsuit have been condemned, for fraud or gross fault, to indemnify the ward.

**II. Rules relating to professions, employments, and public offices**

**Article 498:** The following are also incapable of any guardianship or curatorship:

1. Repealed.
2. Repealed.
3. Those who have to exercise for a long time, or for an indefinite time, a public office or commission outside Chilean territory.

**III. Rules relating to sex**

**Article 499:** Repealed.

**IV. Rules relating to age**

**Article 500:** Those who have not completed twenty-one years may not be guardians or curators.

However, if a guardianship or curatorship is granted to the ascendant or descendant who has not completed twenty-one years, they shall be waited for to reach that age to confer the office, and an interim shall be appointed for the intervening time.

The testamentary guardian or curator who has not completed twenty-one years shall be waited for in the same way. But the appointment of the minor guardian or curator shall be invalid, when upon reaching twenty-one they would only have to exercise the guardianship or curatorship for less than two years.

**Article 501:** When there is no certainty about the age, it shall be judged according to article 314, and if in consequence the office is discerned to the appointed guardian or curator, it shall be valid and subsist, whatever their actual age.

**V. Rules relating to family relationships**

**Article 502:** The stepfather may not be the guardian or curator of his stepchild.

**Article 503:** The husband and wife may not be curators of the other spouse if they are totally separated as to property.

However, this disqualification shall not apply in the case of article 135, in that of conventional separation, nor in the event of a regime of participation in the partnership gains between spouses, in all of which the judge, hearing the relatives, may grant the guardianship to the husband or wife.

**Article 504:** The child may not be curator of their spendthrift father.

**VI. Rules relating to conflict of interests or difference of religion between guardian and ward**

**Article 505:** One who disputes or has disputed a person's civil status may not be their guardian or curator.

**Article 506:** Creditors or debtors of a person, nor those who litigate with them, for their own or others' interests, may not be sole guardians or curators of that person.

The judge, as deemed more convenient, shall add other guardians or curators to administer jointly, or shall declare them incapable of the office.

The spouse and ascendants and descendants of the ward are not subject to the provision of this article.

**Article 507:** The provisions of the preceding article do not include the testamentary guardian or curator, if it is proved that the testator had knowledge of the credit, debt, or litigation at the time of appointing said guardian or curator.

Nor do they extend to credits, debts, or litigation of little importance in the judge's opinion.

**Article 508:** Those who profess a different religion from that in which the ward must be or has been educated, may not be their guardians or curators, except in the case of being accepted by the ascendants, and in their absence by the closest relatives.

**VII. Rules relating to supervening incapacity**

**Article 509:** The aforementioned causes of incapacity, which arise during the exercise of guardianship or curatorship, shall put an end to it.

**Article 510:** The dementia of the guardian or curator shall vitiate with nullity all acts executed by them during it, even if they have not been placed under interdiction.

**Article 511:** If the woman who exercises the guardianship or curatorship marries, she shall continue to perform it, provided that by the fact of marriage the ward is not to be subject to the husband's or wife's parental authority. In this case said guardianship shall cease.

**VIII. General rules on incapacities**

**Article 512:** Guardians or curators who have concealed the causes of incapacity that existed at the time of granting the office or that subsequently arose, in addition to being subject to all the responsibilities of their administration, shall lose the emoluments corresponding to the time in which, knowing the incapacity, they exercised the office.

Unknown causes of incapacity do not vitiate the guardian's or curator's acts; but once known by them, they shall put an end to guardianship or curatorship.

**Article 513:** The guardian who believes themselves incapable of exercising the guardianship or curatorship granted to them, shall have the same periods to provoke the proceeding on their incapacity as those prescribed for the proceeding on their excuses in article 520\.

If incapacity arises during the exercise of guardianship or curatorship, they must denounce it to the judge within three days following the day such incapacity began to exist or came to their knowledge; and this period shall be extended in the same manner as the thirty-day period prescribed in article 520\.

The incapacity of the guardian or curator may also be denounced to the judge by any of the ward's relatives, by their spouse, and even by any member of the community.

payloads.title: § 2\. Of Excuses
§ 3\. Common Rules for Incapacities and Excuses
payloads.content:
**Article 524:** The proceeding on the incapacities or excuses alleged by the guardian shall be conducted with the respective defender.

**Article 525:** If the judge in the first instance does not recognize the causes of incapacity alleged by the guardian, or does not accept their excuses, and if the guardian does not appeal, or if the appeal court confirms the lower judge's ruling, the guardian shall be responsible for any harm resulting to the ward from their delay in taking charge of the guardianship.

This responsibility shall not apply if the guardian or curator, to exempt themselves from it, offers to take interim charge of the guardianship or curatorship.

payloads.title: § 1\. Of Corporeal Things
payloads.content:
**Article 566:** Corporeal things are divided into movable and immovable.

**Article 567:** Movable are those that can be transported from one place to another, whether moving by themselves, such as animals (which for this reason are called semi-movable), or if they only move by an external force, such as inanimate things. Excepted are those which, being movable by nature, are deemed immovable by their destination, according to article 570\.

**Article 568:** Immovable, or estates, or real property, are things that cannot be transported from one place to another; such as lands and mines, and those that permanently adhere to them, such as buildings, trees. Houses and landed estates are called premises or farms.

**Article 569:** Plants are immovable, as long as they adhere to the ground by their roots, unless they are in pots or boxes that can be transported from one place to another.

**Article 570:** Things are deemed immovable, even if by their nature they are not, if they are permanently destined to the use, cultivation, and benefit of an immovable, even though they may be separated without damage. Such are, for example: The slabs of a pavement; The pipes of plumbing; Agricultural or mining tools, and animals actually destined for the cultivation or benefit of an estate, provided they have been placed on it by the owner of the estate; The fertilizers existing on it, and destined by the owner of the estate to improve it; The presses, boilers, vats, stills, barrels, and machines that form part of an industrial establishment attached to the ground, and belong to its owner; The animals kept in rabbitries, aviaries, ponds, beehives, and any other animal enclosures, provided they adhere to the ground, or are part of the ground itself, or of a building.

**Article 571:** The products of immovable property, and things accessory to them, such as grass of a field, wood and fruit of trees, animals in an enclosure, are deemed movable, even before their separation, for the purpose of constituting a right over said products or things to another person than the owner. The same applies to the earth or sand of a soil, the metals of a mine, and the stones of a quarry.

**Article 572:** Things of convenience or ornament that are nailed or fixed in the walls of houses and can be easily removed without damage to the walls, such as stoves, mirrors, pictures, tapestries, are deemed movable. If the pictures or mirrors are embedded in the walls, so as to form one body with them, they shall be considered part of them, even if they can be separated without damage.

**Article 573:** Things that, because they are accessory to real property, are deemed immovable, do not cease to be so by their momentary separation; for example, bulbs or onions that are pulled up to be replanted, and slabs or stones that are removed from their place, to make some construction or repair and with the intention of returning them to it. But from the moment they are separated with the object of giving them a different destination, they cease to be immovable.

**Article 574:** When by law or by man the expression movable property is used without other qualification, it shall include everything understood by movable things, according to article 567\.

In the movable property of a house, money, documents and papers, scientific or artistic collections, books or their shelves, medals, weapons, instruments of arts and crafts, jewelry, clothing and bedding, carriages or horses or their harnesses, grains, wines, merchandise, shall not be included, nor in general other things than those forming the household furniture.

**Article 575:** Movable things are divided into fungible and non-fungible.

To the former belong those of which the use convenient to their nature cannot be made without their being destroyed. Monetary species, insofar as they perish for the one who uses them as such, are fungible things.

payloads.title: § 2\. Of Incorporeal Things
payloads.content:
**Article 576:** Incorporeal things are real or personal rights.

**Article 577:** A real right is one we have over a thing without respect to a determined person. Real rights are those of dominion, inheritance, usufruct, use or habitation, active servitudes, pledge, and mortgage. From these rights arise real actions.

**Article 578:** Personal rights or credits are those that can only be claimed from certain persons, who, by their own act or the sole provision of law, have contracted the correlative obligations; such as the lender has against their debtor for the money lent, or the child against the parent for maintenance. From these rights arise personal actions.

**Article 579:** The right of ground rent is personal insofar as it can be directed against the rent charge debtor, even if not in possession of the charged estate, and real insofar as the estate is pursued.

**Article 580:** Rights and actions are deemed movable or immovable property, according to whether the thing on which they are to be exercised, or which is owed, is movable or immovable. Thus the right of usufruct over an immovable is immovable. Thus the buyer's action for delivery of the purchased estate is immovable; and the action of the one who lent money, to be paid, is movable.

**Article 581:** Acts that are owed are deemed movable. The action for a craftsman to perform the agreed work, or to compensate for damages caused by non-performance of the agreement, therefore belongs to the class of movable property.

payloads.title: § 1\. Of Accessions of Fruits
payloads.content:
**Article 644:** Natural fruits are those given by nature aided or not by human industry.

**Article 645:** Natural fruits are called pending while they still adhere to the thing that produces them, such as plants rooted in the soil, or products of plants while they have not been separated from them.

Natural fruits are called perceived when they have been separated from the productive thing, such as cut timber, harvested fruits and grains, etc.; and they are said to be consumed when they have been truly consumed or have been alienated.

**Article 646:** Natural fruits of a thing belong to its owner; without prejudice to the rights constituted by laws, or by an act of man, for the possessor in good faith, the usufructuary, the lessee.

Thus the vegetation that the land produces spontaneously or by cultivation, and the fruits, seeds, and other products of vegetation, belong to the owner of the land.

Thus also skins, wool, horns, milk, offspring, and other products of animals belong to their owner.

**Article 647:** Civil fruits are the prices, pensions, or rents of leases or ground rents, and the interest of demandable capital, or imposed as a charge on property.

Civil fruits are called pending while they are owed; and perceived from when they are collected.

**Article 648:** Civil fruits also belong to the owner of the thing from which they come, in the same manner and with the same limitation as natural fruits.

payloads.title: § 2\. Of Accessions of the Soil
payloads.content:
**Article 649:** Alluvion is the increase received by the bank of the sea or of a river or lake by the slow and imperceptible retreat of the waters.

**Article 650:** Alluvion land accedes to riparian estates within their respective boundary lines prolonged directly to the water; but in habilitated ports it shall belong to the State.

The soil that the water occupies and vacates alternately in its periodic rises and falls forms part of the bank or bed, and does not accede in the meantime to the adjoining estates.

**Article 651:** Whenever the aforesaid boundary lines, prolonged, intersect each other before reaching the water, the triangle formed by them and by the water's edge shall accede to the two lateral estates; a straight line dividing it into two equal parts, drawn from the point of intersection to the water, shall be the dividing line between the two estates.

**Article 652:** Over the part of the soil that by a flood or other violent natural force is transported from one place to another, the owner retains their ownership, for the sole purpose of taking it away; but if they do not claim it within the following year, the owner of the place to which it was transported shall make it theirs.

**Article 653:** If an estate has been flooded, the land restored by the waters within the following five years shall return to its former owners.

**Article 654:** If a river changes its course, the riparian proprietors, with permission of competent authority, may do the necessary works to restore the waters to their accustomed channel; and the part of the latter that permanently remains dry shall accede to the adjoining estates, like alluvion land in the case of article 650\.

If the riparian proprietors on one side meet with those on the other, a longitudinal line shall divide the new land into two equal parts; and each of these shall accede to the adjoining estates, as in the case of the same article.

**Article 655:** If a river divides into two branches that do not later rejoin, the parts of the previous bed that the water leaves uncovered shall accede to the adjoining estates, as in the case of the preceding article.

**Article 656:** Regarding new islands that are not to belong to the State according to article 597, the following rules shall be observed:

1. The new island shall be regarded as part of the riverbed, as long as it is alternately occupied and vacated by the waters in their periodic rises and falls, and shall not accede in the meantime to the riparian estates.

2. The new island formed by a river that opens into two branches that later rejoin does not alter the previous ownership of the lands comprised in it; but the new land uncovered by the river shall accede to the adjoining estates, as in the case of article 654\.

3. The new island formed in the bed of a river shall accede to the estates of that one of the two banks to which the entire island is closest; each estate corresponding to the part between its respective boundary lines prolonged directly to the island and over its surface.

If the entire island is not closer to one of the two banks than to the other, it shall accede to the estates of both banks; each estate corresponding to the part between its respective boundary lines prolonged directly to the island and over its surface.

The parts of the island that by virtue of these provisions correspond to two or more estates shall be divided in equal parts among the common estates.

4. For the distribution of a new island, any island or islands that pre-existed it shall be entirely disregarded; and the new island shall accede to the riparian estates as if it alone existed.

5. Owners of an island formed by the river acquire ownership of everything by alluvion that accedes to it, whatever bank the new land abandoned by the waters is less distant from.

6. To the new island formed in a lake, paragraph 2 of rule 3 above shall apply; but estates whose lesser distance from the island exceeds half the diameter of the island, measured in the direction of that same distance, shall not have a share in the division of the land formed by the waters.

payloads.title: § 3\. Of Accession of One Movable Thing to Another
payloads.content:
**Article 657:** Adjunction is a species of accession, and occurs when two movable things belonging to different owners are joined one to another, but in such a way that they can be separated and each subsist after separation; such as when the diamond of one person is set in the gold of another, or in another's frame a mirror of one's own is placed.

**Article 658:** In cases of adjunction, without knowledge of the fact on one side, nor bad faith on the other, the ownership of the accessory shall accede to the ownership of the principal, with the burden of paying the owner of the accessory part its value.

**Article 659:** If of the two united things one is of much greater value than the other, the former shall be regarded as the principal and the latter as the accessory.

The thing that has for its owner a great sentimental value shall be regarded as of greater value.

**Article 660:** If there is not so much difference in value, that one of the two things which serves for the use, ornament, or complement of the other shall be considered accessory.

**Article 661:** In cases to which none of the preceding rules can be applied, the larger in volume shall be regarded as principal.

**Article 662:** Another species of accession is specification, which occurs when from material belonging to one person, another person makes a work or artifact of any kind, such as if from another's grapes wine is made, or from another's silver a cup, or from another's wood a ship.

Without knowledge of the fact on one side, nor bad faith on the other, the owner of the material shall have the right to claim the new species, paying for the workmanship.

Unless in the work or artifact the price of the new species is worth much more than that of the material, such as when a painting is made on another's canvas, or a statue from another's marble; in which case the new species shall belong to the specifier, and the owner of the material shall only have the right to damages.

If the material of the artifact is, in part, another's, and, in part, the own of the one who made or had it made, and the two parts cannot be separated without inconvenience, the species shall belong in common to the two proprietors; to one in proportion to the value of their material, and to the other in proportion to the value of theirs and the workmanship.

**Article 663:** If a thing is formed by mixture of dry or liquid materials belonging to different owners, without knowledge of the fact on one side, nor bad faith on the other, the ownership of the thing shall belong to said owners in common, in proportion to the value of the material belonging to each.

Unless the value of the material belonging to one of them is considerably higher, in which case the owner of it shall have the right to claim the thing produced by the mixture, paying the price of the remaining material.

**Article 664:** In all cases where it is not easy for the owner of one of the two united materials to replace it with another of the same quality, value, and fitness, and the first can be separated without damage to the rest, the owner of it, without whose knowledge the union was made, may demand its separation and delivery, at the cost of the one who used it.

**Article 665:** In all cases where the owner of a material that has been used without their knowledge has the right to the property of the thing in which it has been employed, they shall also have the right to demand that in place of said material they be returned an equal amount of the same nature, quality, and fitness, or its value in money.

**Article 666:** One who has had knowledge of the use that another person was making of their material shall be presumed to have consented and shall only have the right to its value.

**Article 667:** One who has used another's material without the owner's knowledge, and without just cause of error, shall in all cases be subject to losing their own, and to paying what more than this the damages inflicted on the owner are worth; besides the criminal action that may apply, when they have proceeded knowingly.

If the value of the work notably exceeds that of the material, the provision of the preceding paragraph shall not apply; except when knowingly proceeded.

payloads.title: § 4\. Of Accession of Movable Things to Immovable Things
payloads.content:
**Article 668:** If one builds with another's materials on their own land, the owner of the land shall become owner of the materials by the fact of incorporating them into the construction; but shall be obliged to pay the owner of the materials their fair price, or an equal amount of the same nature, quality, and fitness.

If on their part there was no just cause of error, they shall be obliged to reparation of damages, and if they proceeded knowingly, shall also be subject to the competent criminal action; but if the owner of the materials had knowledge of the use being made of them, only the provision of the preceding paragraph shall apply.

The same rule applies to one who plants or sows on their own land another's vegetables or seeds.

While the materials are not incorporated into the construction or the vegetables rooted in the ground, the owner may claim them.

**Article 669:** The owner of the land in which another person, without their knowledge, has built, planted, or sown, shall have the right to make the building, planting, or sowing their own, upon payment of the indemnities prescribed in favor of possessors in good or bad faith in the title On reclamation, or to oblige the one who built or planted to pay them the fair price of the land with legal interest for all the time they have had it in their power, and the one who sowed to pay them the rent and indemnify them for damages.

If building, planting, or sowing has been done with the knowledge and acquiescence of the landowner, they shall be obliged, to recover it, to pay the value of the building, planting, or sowing.

payloads.title: § 1\. General Provisions
payloads.content:
**Article 670:** Tradition is a mode of acquiring the dominion of things and consists of the delivery that the owner makes of them to another, having on the one hand the faculty and intention to transfer the dominion, and on the other the capacity and intention to acquire it.

What is said of dominion extends to all other real rights.

**Article 671:** The person who by tradition transfers the dominion of the thing delivered by them or in their name is called the tradent, and the person who by tradition acquires the dominion of the thing received by them or in their name is called the acquirer.

Their attorneys or legal representatives may deliver and receive in the name of the owner.

In forced sales made by judicial decree at the request of a creditor, at public auction, the person whose dominion is transferred is the tradent, and the judge their legal representative.

Tradition made by or to an attorney duly authorized is understood to be made by or to the respective principal.

**Article 672:** For tradition to be valid, it must be made voluntarily by the tradent or by their representative.

A tradition that was initially invalid for having been made without the will of the tradent or their representative, is validated retroactively by the ratification of the one who has the power to alienate the thing as owner or as representative of the owner.

**Article 673:** Tradition, to be valid, also requires the consent of the acquirer or their representative. But the tradition that was initially invalid for lack of this consent is validated retroactively by ratification.

**Article 674:** For tradition to be valid in which attorneys or legal representatives intervene, it is also required that they act within the limits of their mandate or their legal representation.

**Article 675:** For tradition to be valid, a translative title of dominion is required, such as sale, exchange, donation, etc.

It is also required that the title be valid with respect to the person to whom it is conferred. Thus the title of irrevocable donation does not transfer dominion between spouses.

**Article 676:** It is also required for the validity of tradition that there be no error regarding the identity of the species to be delivered, or of the person to whom the delivery is made, nor regarding the title.

If there is error only in the name, the tradition is valid.

**Article 677:** Error in the title invalidates tradition, whether when only one of the parties supposes a translative title of dominion, such as when on the one hand there is the intention to deliver by way of loan for use, and on the other the intention to receive by way of donation, or whether when both parties suppose translative titles of dominion, but different, such as if on the one hand loan for consumption is supposed, and on the other donation.

**Article 678:** If the tradition is made by means of attorneys or legal representatives, the error of these invalidates the tradition.

**Article 679:** If the law requires special formalities for alienation, dominion is not transferred without them.

**Article 680:** Tradition may transfer dominion under suspensive or resolutory condition, provided it is expressed.

Once delivery is made by the seller, the dominion of the thing sold is transferred, even if the price has not been paid, unless the seller has reserved dominion until payment, or until fulfillment of a condition.

**Article 681:** The tradition of everything owed may be demanded, as long as there is no pending term for its payment; unless a judicial decree intervenes to the contrary.

**Article 682:** If the tradent is not the true owner of the thing delivered by them or in their name, no other rights are acquired by means of tradition than the transmissible rights of the same tradent over the thing delivered.

But if the tradent subsequently acquires the dominion, it shall be understood to have been transferred from the moment of tradition.

**Article 683:** Tradition gives the acquirer, in the cases and in the manner that the laws indicate, the right to gain by prescription the dominion that the tradent lacked, even if the tradent did not have that right.

payloads.title: § 2\. Of Tradition of Corporeal Movable Things
§ 3\. Of Other Species of Tradition
payloads.content:
**Article 686:** Tradition of the dominion of real property shall be effected by the registration of the title in the Registrar's Registry. In the same manner, tradition of the rights of usufruct or use constituted over real property, of the rights of habitation or ground rent, and of the right of mortgage shall be effected.

Regarding the tradition of mines, the provisions of the Mining Code shall apply.

**Article 687:** The registration of the title of dominion and of any other of the real rights mentioned in the preceding article shall be made in the Registrar's Registry of the territory in which the immovable is situated, and if it belongs to several territories by location, the registration shall be made in the Registry of each of them.

If the title relates to two or more immovable properties, it shall be registered in the Registrar's Registries of all the territories to which they belong by location.

If by a partition act, the immovable properties or part of the immovable properties that were previously possessed in common are adjudicated to several persons, the partition act relating to each immovable or each adjudicated part shall be registered in the Registrar's Registry in whose territory the immovable is located.

**Article 688:** At the moment the inheritance is granted, effective possession of it is conferred by operation of law to the heir; but this legal possession does not enable the heir to dispose in any way of an immovable, as long as there does not precede:

1. The registration of the judicial decree or the administrative resolution granting effective possession: the former before the registrar of real property of the commune or grouping of communes in which it was pronounced, together with the corresponding will, and the latter in the National Registry of Effective Possessions;
2. The special registrations provided in the first and second paragraphs of the preceding article: by virtue of them, the heirs may jointly dispose of the hereditary immovable property, and
3. The registration provided in paragraph three: without this, the heir may not dispose by themselves of the hereditary immovable property that fell to them in the partition.

**Article 689:** Whenever by a final judgment dominion or any other of the rights mentioned in articles 686 and following is recognized as acquired by prescription, this judgment shall serve as title, and shall be registered in the respective Registry or Registries.

**Article 690:** To carry out the registration, an authentic copy of the respective title, and of the judicial decree if applicable, shall be exhibited to the Registrar.

The registration shall begin with the date of this act; shall express the nature and date of the title, the names, surnames, and domiciles of the parties, and the designation of the thing, according to all appearing in the title; shall also express the office or archive where the original title is kept; and shall end with the Registrar's signature.

**Article 691:** The registration of a will shall include the date of its execution; the name, surname, and domicile of the testator; the names, surnames, and domiciles of the heirs or legatees requesting the registration, expressing their shares, or the respective legacies.

The registration of a judgment or decree shall include its date, the designation of the respective court or tribunal, and a literal copy of the dispositive part.

The registration of a legal act of partition shall include the date of this act, the name and surname of the judge-partitioner, and the designation of the parts or lots belonging to those requesting the registration.

The aforementioned registrations shall conform in other respects to the provisions of the preceding article.

**Article 692:** Whenever a right that has been previously registered is transferred, the previous registration shall be mentioned in the new one.

**Article 693:** For the transfer, by donation or contract between living persons, of the ownership of an estate that has not been previously registered, the Registrar shall require proof that notice of said transfer has been given to the public by means of three notices published in a newspaper of the commune or of the capital of the province or of the capital of the region, if there is none in the commune, and by a poster posted for at least fifteen days in the office of the respective Registrar of Real Property.

The same rule shall apply to the constitution or transfer by act between living persons of the other real rights mentioned in the preceding articles, and relating to unregistered immovable property.

**Article 694:** If the registration refers to minutes or documents not kept in the registry or protocol of a public office, said minutes or documents shall be kept in the Registrar's archive, under their custody and responsibility.

**Article 695:** A special regulation shall determine in other respects the duties and functions of the Registrar, and the form and solemnity of registrations.

**Article 696:** Titles whose registration is prescribed in the preceding articles shall not give or transfer effective possession of the respective right, as long as registration is not effected in the manner ordered in said articles; but this provision shall only apply with respect to titles granted after the period indicated in the aforementioned regulation.

**Article 697:** In the intervening time between the date this Code begins to govern and that in which registration becomes obligatory, registration of the real rights mentioned in the preceding articles shall be made in the following manner:

1. That of a right of dominion, usufruct, use, or habitation, by means of a public deed in which the tradent expresses delivering it, and the acquirer receiving it: this deed may be the same as the act or contract by which the right is transferred or constituted;
2. That of a right of mortgage or ground rent, by annotation in the competent mortgage office;
3. That of a right of inheritance, by the judicial decree granting effective possession;
4. That of a legacy, by means of a public deed like that provided in number 1; and
5. That of the object adjudicated in a partition act, by public deed in which the adjudication and the adjudicatee's acceptance appear.

**Article 698:** Tradition of a right of servitude shall be effected by public deed in which the tradent expresses constituting it, and the acquirer accepting it: this deed may be the same as the act or contract.

**Article 699:** Tradition of personal rights that an individual assigns to another is effected by delivery of the title made by the assignor to the assignee.

**Article 691:** The registration of a will shall include the date of its execution; the name, surname, and domicile of the testator; the names, surnames, and domiciles of the heirs or legatees requesting the registration, expressing their shares, or the respective legacies.

The registration of a judgment or decree shall include its date, the designation of the respective court or tribunal, and a literal copy of the dispositive part.

The registration of a legal act of partition shall include the date of this act, the name and surname of the judge-partitioner, and the designation of the parts or lots belonging to those requesting the registration.

The aforementioned registrations shall conform in other respects to the provisions of the preceding article.

**Article 692:** Whenever a right that has been previously registered is transferred, the previous registration shall be mentioned in the new one.

**Article 693:** For the transfer, by donation or contract between living persons, of the ownership of an estate that has not been previously registered, the Registrar shall require proof that notice of said transfer has been given to the public by means of three notices published in a newspaper of the commune or of the capital of the province or of the capital of the region, if there is none in the commune, and by a poster posted for at least fifteen days in the office of the respective Registrar of Real Property.

The same rule shall apply to the constitution or transfer by act between living persons of the other real rights mentioned in the preceding articles, and relating to unregistered immovable property.

**Article 694:** If the registration refers to minutes or documents not kept in the registry or protocol of a public office, said minutes or documents shall be kept in the Registrar's archive, under their custody and responsibility.

**Article 695:** A special regulation shall determine in other respects the duties and functions of the Registrar, and the form and solemnity of registrations.

**Article 696:** Titles whose registration is prescribed in the preceding articles shall not give or transfer effective possession of the respective right, as long as registration is not effected in the manner ordered in said articles; but this provision shall only apply with respect to titles granted after the period indicated in the aforementioned regulation.

**Article 697:** In the intervening time between the date this Code begins to govern and that in which registration becomes obligatory, registration of the real rights mentioned in the preceding articles shall be made in the following manner:

1. That of a right of dominion, usufruct, use, or habitation, by means of a public deed in which the tradent expresses delivering it, and the acquirer receiving it: this deed may be the same as the act or contract by which the right is transferred or constituted;
2. That of a right of mortgage or ground rent, by annotation in the competent mortgage office;
3. That of a right of inheritance, by the judicial decree granting effective possession;
4. That of a legacy, by means of a public deed like that provided in number 1; and
5. That of the object adjudicated in a partition act, by public deed in which the adjudication and the adjudicatee's acceptance appear.

**Article 698:** Tradition of a right of servitude shall be effected by public deed in which the tradent expresses constituting it, and the acquirer accepting it: this deed may be the same as the act or contract.

**Article 699:** Tradition of personal rights that an individual assigns to another is effected by delivery of the title made by the assignor to the assignee.

payloads.title: § 1\. Of Possession and Its Different Qualities
payloads.content:
**Article 700:** Possession is the holding of a determined thing with the intention of lord or owner, whether the owner or the one who holds themselves as such has the thing by themselves, or through another person who holds it in their place and name.

The possessor is reputed owner, as long as another person does not justify being so.

**Article 701:** One may possess a thing by several titles.

**Article 702:** Possession may be regular or irregular.

Regular possession is that which proceeds from a just title and has been acquired in good faith; although good faith does not subsist after possession is acquired. One can therefore be a regular possessor and a possessor in bad faith, as conversely the possessor in good faith may be an irregular possessor.

If the title is translative of dominion, tradition is also necessary.

Possession of a thing with the knowledge and acquiescence of the one who obliged themselves to deliver it shall create a presumption of tradition; unless this should have been effected by registration of the title.

**Article 703:** Just title is constitutive or translative of dominion.

Occupation, accession, and prescription are constitutive of dominion.

Transpositive of dominion are those that by their nature serve to transfer it, such as sale, exchange, donation between living persons.

Belonging to this class are judgments of adjudication in divisory lawsuits, and legal acts of partition.

Judicial judgments on litigious rights do not form a new title to legitimize possession.

Transactions insofar as they are limited to recognizing or declaring pre-existing rights do not form a new title; but insofar as they transfer the property of an undisputed object, they constitute a new title.

**Article 704:** The following are not just title:

1. Counterfeit, that is, not actually granted by the person pretended;
2. Granted by a person as attorney or legal representative of another without being so;
3. That suffers from a defect of nullity, such as alienation that should have been authorized by a legal representative or by judicial decree and has not been; and
4. Merely putative, such as the apparent heir who is not really an heir; the legatee whose legacy has been revoked by a later testamentary act, etc.

However, the putative heir to whom effective possession has been granted by judicial decree or administrative resolution shall be served by the decree or resolution as just title; as the putative legatee by the corresponding testamentary act that has been legally executed.

**Article 705:** The validation of the title that in its principle was null, effected by ratification, or by another legal means, retroacts to the date the title was granted.

**Article 706:** Good faith is the consciousness of having acquired the dominion of the thing by legitimate means, free from fraud and any other defect.

Thus in translative titles of dominion, good faith supposes the persuasion of having received the thing from the one who had the faculty to alienate it, and that there has been no fraud or other defect in the act or contract.

A just error in a matter of fact does not oppose good faith.

But error in a matter of law constitutes a presumption of bad faith, which admits no contrary proof.

**Article 707:** Good faith is presumed, except in cases where the law establishes the contrary presumption. In all others, bad faith must be proved.

**Article 708:** Irregular possession is that which lacks one or more of the requirements indicated in article 702\.

**Article 709:** Vicious possessions are violent and clandestine.

**Article 710:** Violent possession is that acquired by force. Force may be actual or imminent.

**Article 711:** One who in the owner's absence takes possession of the thing, and upon the owner's return repels them, is also a violent possessor.

**Article 712:** The vice of violence exists, whether it has been employed against the true owner of the thing, or against the one who possessed it without being so, or against the one who held it in the place or name of another.

It is the same whether the violence is executed by one person or by their agents, and whether it is executed with their consent or if after executed it is ratified expressly or tacitly.

**Article 713:** Clandestine possession is that exercised by hiding it from those who have the right to oppose it.

**Article 714:** Mere holding is that exercised over a thing, not as owner, but in the place or name of the owner. The pledge creditor, the sequestrator, the usufructuary, the user, the one who has the right of habitation, are mere holders of the pledged, sequestered thing, or whose usufruct, use, or habitation belongs to them.

The foregoing applies generally to everyone who holds a thing recognizing another's dominion.

**Article 715:** Possession of incorporeal things is susceptible to the same qualities and vices as possession of a corporeal thing.

**Article 716:** The mere lapse of time does not change mere holding into possession; except in the case of article 2510, rule 3\.

**Article 717:** Whether one succeeds by universal or singular title, the successor's possession begins in them; unless they wish to add their predecessor's possession to theirs; but in such case, they appropriate it with its qualities and vices.

To one's own possession may also be added in the same terms that of a continuous series of predecessors.

**Article 718:** Each of the co-owners of a thing possessed in common shall be understood to have possessed exclusively the part that fell to them by division, during all the time the indivision lasted.

They may therefore add this time to their exclusive possession, and the alienations they have made by themselves of the common thing and the real rights with which they have encumbered it shall subsist over said part if it was included in the alienation or encumbrance. But if what was alienated or encumbered extended to more, the alienation or encumbrance shall not subsist against the will of the respective adjudicatees.

**Article 719:** If one has begun to possess in one's own name, it is presumed that this possession has continued until the moment it is alleged.

If one has begun to possess in another's name, the continuation of the same order of things is equally presumed.

If someone proves having possessed previously, and possesses currently, possession in the intervening time is presumed.

**Article 720:** Possession may be taken not only by the one who seeks to acquire it for themselves, but by their attorney, or by their legal representatives.

payloads.title: § 2\. Of the Modes of Acquiring and Losing Possession
payloads.content:
**Article 721:** If a person takes possession of a thing in the place or name of another of whom they are attorney or legal representative, the possession of the principal or represented begins in the same act, even without their knowledge.

If the one who takes possession in another's name is not their attorney or representative, the latter shall not possess except by virtue of their knowledge and acceptance; but their possession shall retroact to the moment it was taken in their name.

**Article 722:** Possession of the inheritance is acquired from the moment it is granted, even if the heir is unaware of it.

One who validly repudiates an inheritance is understood never to have possessed it.

**Article 723:** Those who cannot freely administer their own property do not need any authorization to acquire possession of a movable thing, provided that will and material or legal apprehension concur; but they cannot exercise the rights of possessors except with the appropriate authorization.

The demented and infants are incapable of acquiring possession by their will, either for themselves or for others.

**Article 724:** If the thing is one of those whose tradition must be made by registration in the Registrar's Registry, no one may acquire possession of it except by this means.

**Article 725:** The possessor retains possession, even if they transfer the holding of the thing, giving it in lease, loan for use, pledge, deposit, usufruct, or by any other non-translative title of dominion.

**Article 726:** One ceases to possess a thing from the moment another takes possession of it with the intention of making it their own; except in cases the laws expressly except.

**Article 727:** Possession of a movable thing is not understood to be lost as long as it remains in the possessor's power, even if they accidentally ignore its whereabouts.

**Article 728:** For registered possession to cease, the registration must be cancelled, either by will of the parties, or by a new registration in which the registered possessor transfers their right to another, or by judicial decree.

As long as the registration subsists, the one who takes possession of the thing to which the registered title refers does not acquire possession of it nor put an end to the existing possession.

**Article 729:** If someone, claiming to be owner, violently or clandestinely takes possession of an immovable whose title is not registered, the one who had possession loses it.

**Article 730:** If the one who holds the thing in the place and name of another usurps it, giving themselves as owner, possession is not lost on one side nor acquired on the other; unless the usurper alienates the thing in their own name. In this case, the person to whom it is alienated acquires possession of the thing and puts an end to the previous possession.

However, if the one who holds the thing in the place and name of a registered possessor gives themselves as owner and alienates it, possession is not lost on one side nor acquired on the other without the competent registration.

**Article 731:** One who legally recovers lost possession shall be understood to have had it during all the intervening time.

payloads.title: § 1\. Of Natural Servitudes
payloads.content:
**Article 833:** The lower estate is subject to receiving the waters that descend from the upper estate naturally, that is, without the hand of man contributing to it.

One may not therefore direct a drain or ditch over the neighboring estate, if this special servitude has not been constituted.

On the servient estate, nothing may be done that hinders the natural servitude, nor on the dominant estate, that aggravates it.

The servitudes established in this article shall be governed by the Water Code.

**Articles 834-838:** Repealed.
